title: The Order of Resurrection and the Kingdom
english: The second catena form adds: “In Adam” stands for “because of Adam,” just as “in Christ” stands for “because of Christ.” So in Adam we die, clearly in the body, and in Christ they will be made alive, clearly in the body. If souls were alive before Christ, and after Christ it is again only souls that live, what did the saving plan add?

On 1 Corinthians 15:23–25: By “order” he means the order of the righteous and of the unrighteous. Here “those who are Christ's” does not mean the faithful in particular, but everyone, because all are Christ's. At his coming there will be the resurrection of all, when the end also comes: the drowning of death and of the devil, for this is the end of the world. By “the kingdom” he means not his own, but the one the evil one seized when he brought down Adam and those descended from him. In handing this kingdom over to the Father he will not be a stranger to it, for the Son reigns together with the Father. “Reign until” does not mark a time limit but emphasis, as if someone were to say, “I must live virtuously until I achieve righteousness.” He does not mean that once I have achieved it I will no longer live in righteousness, but that righteousness has to be achieved by me through virtuous effort. In the prophets too, “until” does not always mark a limit but emphasis, as in the Old Testament where he says, “I am, I am, until you grow old” (Isaiah 46:4). He does not say that the old age of those who grow old is the limit of his being, but that even when you grow old, I am: not growing old with you, but always being. So here too “until” marks the goal reached. What he means is this: his kingdom will not be broken off in the meantime, nor will believers fail, until what he purposed has been accomplished; and once he has accomplished it, he will reign without end.

On 1 Corinthians 15:29: If the bodies, he says, stay dead and do not rise, why are we baptized for these dead, as though they would rise and be judged, receiving forgiveness of sins so as not to be condemned?
On 1 Corinthians 15:32: As far as man could do it, he says, I fought with wild beasts, but God saved me.

On 1 Corinthians 15:35–38: The Greeks object that a seed once split no longer sprouts, and so neither is a man raised again if his foot has been cut off or his body maimed altogether. They do not know that the comparison is not of one nature with another, but with the power of the Maker. That is, who gave the seed its nature to sprout and its power as seed? Was it not God? Who makes the seed first die and then rise? Is it not God?

title: The distinction between nature and choice in resurrection
english: So he who gave the grain its power as seed has also given our bodies the strength to rise. I did not bring in the body of crops and of men as though they were alike, but to set before you the Creator's power.

On 1 Corinthians 15:40–42: Not as though the other kinds of flesh rise; he is using an illustration. By “heavenly bodies” he means the sun and the moon, and what follows shows it: “So also is the resurrection of the dead.” You see that what came first was an illustration; now he has given the thing the illustration was for.

On 1 Corinthians 15:44: By the body “of the soul” he means the body put to death by the soul's sin, and by the “spiritual” body the one raised by the power of the Spirit. That body will no longer live by the weakness of the soul, which is not strong enough to hold the body's frame together, but by the power of the Spirit, which carries it over into immortality.

On 1 Corinthians 15:45: This is what Moses says: “And the man became a living soul” (Genesis 2:7). The second man became a life-giving spirit. This is what the Gospel says: “For what has been conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 1:20).
On 1 Corinthians 15:47: Man is “from the earth” by nature, and “earthy” by choice. He says that Christ is “from heaven”: not by likeness; nor does eternity come from resurrection.

On 1 Corinthians 15:47–49: The followers of Valentinus and Marcion, the followers of Photinus and those of Apollinarius all run to this text, but the passage refutes them all. I ask: did the earthy man from the earth have a soul or not? They will not deny it. And the Lord from heaven had a body from the earth. Again I ask: why does he call the first man “from the earth, earthy,” but the Lord “from heaven”? And after that, “As is the earthy” (and he no longer mentions earth, but says) “so are those who are earthy”? Clearly because “from the earth” belongs to nature, while “earthy” belongs to choice. When he comes to “as is the earthy,” and is accusing those who have not lived well, he no longer mentions nature or “from the earth,” and he no longer calls the Lord “from heaven” but “heavenly.” Again, the spiritual too were from the earth. “As is the earthy, so are those who are earthy, and as is the heavenly, so are those who are heavenly.” And it follows of necessity: if some deny that the Lord from heaven took flesh, because he is from heaven, they must also refuse to grant that the heavenly ones took a body, since “as is the earthy, so are those who are earthy.” And so this stands on no ground at all if it is understood…

title: The Nature of Resurrection and Transformation
english: …otherwise than this: he spoke of nature, which is why he says “from the earth.” From the earth come both the heavenly ones and those called earthy, but the two are no longer both earthy. So we must notice that the Lord is said to be “from heaven,” not the heavenly ones, and that the heavenly ones are from the earth, not the Lord from heaven. By “the image of the earthy” he means the earthy way of living, and by “the image of the heavenly” the heavenly way of life. That is: we copied Adam's disobedience; let us also copy the obedience of the Son of God by obeying.

On 1 Corinthians 15:50: Many of the heretics, in their great folly, drag this text against the resurrection. But he did not say that flesh and blood do not rise; he said that they “will not inherit the kingdom of God.” He shut them out of the kingdom of the Son of God, not out of the grace of the resurrection. What he means is this: flesh, while it is flesh, does not inherit, and blood, while it is blood, does not inherit. As long as flesh is flesh, it is perishable; but once it has put on incorruption and laid aside the weakness of the flesh, it becomes something else, that is, imperishable. He has proved what he said before. He calls the kingdom “incorruption,” and “corruption” the mortality of this age. Opposites do not become heirs of their opposites.

On 1 Corinthians 15:52: He made clear that there are many trumpets, for by mentioning the last he implied the first ones too. “And the dead will be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed.” If the dead are incorruptible, clearly they too will be changed. What need, then, for “and we shall be changed”? Surely he said “incorruptible” of everyone alike, while “we shall be changed” now hints at the change for the better. That is why he said “we,” of the righteous.

The second catena form adds: By saying this and pointing to the body, he hemmed in the heretics who say there is a resurrection not of the flesh but of the soul. These people are impious even about the divine plan itself, supposing that Christ took flesh not in truth but in appearance, which is senseless. If he had no flesh, what was it that died and was buried and rose? And if these things happened in appearance, then we too die in appearance. The “we” would be superfluous, unless perhaps he means it to point to the saints, standing for “the righteous among us,” just as elsewhere, by saying “we who are alive” (1 Thessalonians 4:17), he pointed to the saints around him.
On 1 Corinthians 16:1: “Collection” is the name for a contribution made by gathering money, for the relief of the poor.
